title: Catherine of Siena, saint and stateswoman
gist: Eloise Davies portrays Catherine of Siena (d. 1380 aged 33) as a political thinker who used the language of carità (love of neighbour as divine duty) as an alternative to factional violence in Italian city states, and who helped persuade Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome.

insights.claim: Catherine of Siena, usually remembered as saint and mystic, was one of the most politically influential women of the early Italian Renaissance, credited by Catholic tradition with persuading Pope Gregory XI to end the papacy's Avignon exile (1309-76).
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Shows informal, non-office-holding actors can move major institutional decisions; relevant to how influence is mapped historically.
insights.locator: Though usually remembered as a saint and mystic

insights.claim: When letters urging Gregory to return did not work, Catherine travelled to Avignon to argue in person, and the return to Rome was a moment of papal triumph and an escape from an interfering French monarchy.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Papal-French rivalry shaped the geopolitics of the late medieval church.
insights.locator: The most powerful figure with whom Catherine corresponded

insights.claim: Entering the mantellate, a lay Dominican group, gave Catherine unusual freedom of manoeuvre to travel and write to powerful figures such as Bernabò Visconti of Milan and the English condottiere Sir John Hawkwood.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Institutional form (lay status) can enable more access than formal office.
insights.locator: she was received into the mantellate

insights.claim: Catherine took sides in major controversies: she backed the papacy against Florence in the War of the Eight Saints (1375-78) and favoured the Italian choice over the French in the disputed papal elections of 1378.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Illustrates that religious figures acted as partisans in interstate conflicts.

insights.claim: Catherine wrote letters persuading Tuscan cities to join the papal side while Florentine Chancellor Coluccio Salutati wrote public letters persuading them to ally with Florence, so Catherine and early Florentine humanists inhabited the same political world.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Letter-writing campaigns were the era's tool of influence operations.
insights.locator: When the Florentine Chancellor Coluccio Salutati

insights.claim: Catherine's writings centre on carità, the love of God expressed as love of neighbour, which in a civic context made love of fellow citizens a divine duty and meant religious life required participation in city life rather than pure contemplation.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: A civic-virtue framework tying moral obligation to political participation.
insights.locator: Catherine’s writings about city life revolve around the concept of carità

insights.claim: Acting with carità meant setting aside one's own interests for civic harmony, a rhetorically potent language in cramped cities where opposing factions lived side by side and one faction would often forcibly expel another and seize its property.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Factional expulsion and property seizure cycles destabilised city states.
insights.locator: Acting with carità meant putting aside one’s own interests

insights.claim: Expulsions and seizures rarely solved problems for long: exiled factions camped near the city awaiting readmission and possibly violent revenge, as in the White and Black Guelf conflict that drove Dante out of Florence, and legal disputes over property could drag on for years.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Zero-sum factional politics generates persistent instability, a lesson for contested property regimes.
insights.locator: Expulsions and seizures rarely solved problems

insights.claim: Goodwill above the legal minimum was often needed to end civic disturbances, and Catherine developed carità as a political alternative.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Legal settlement alone is insufficient for durable reconciliation.
insights.locator: Those with experience of such acrimony

insights.claim: Catherine contrasted with Franciscan ideals of virtuous poverty: for her the physical and thus political world mattered, so questions of property, jurisdiction and rule could not be ignored but should be exercised charitably.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: A pro-engagement stance on property and governance against ascetic withdrawal.
insights.locator: also contrasted with the ideas of virtuous poverty

insights.claim: In her Dialogo della Divina Providenza, God distributes virtues so that no one person has all of them, requiring citizens to exercise their virtues for each other; as Catherine says, 'every virtue and every vice is put into action by means of your neighbours'.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Interdependence of citizens is the foundation of her civic ethics.
insights.quote: every virtue and every vice is put into action by means of your neighbours
insights.locator: In this work – the fullest statement of her thought

insights.claim: Florence and Siena enjoyed forms of republican self-government resembling modern democracies, in which a wide mercantile elite debated politics and competed for power, and in the 1920s historian Hans Baron turned to this period to defend Weimar Germany.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Historians use city-state republicanism as a template for participatory politics.
insights.locator: Florence and Siena enjoyed forms of republican self-government

insights.claim: Catherine left roughly 300 surviving letters and her Dialogo, in which she adapted Thomas Aquinas for a broader civic audience.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Documents the scale of her surviving political and theological output.

insights.claim: Catherine's iconography links her to books: Bellini paired her with Aquinas, Pinturicchio painted her canonisation by Pius II, and Aldus Manutius's 1500 edition of her letters included a woodcut that was the first use of italic type in print history.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Print and visual culture amplified her reputation; early italic type debut.
insights.locator: In 1500, the pioneering Venetian printer Aldus Manutius

insights.claim: Edward Gibbon mocked the idea of 'visionary females' influencing popes, while the papacy continued to display Vasari's depiction of Catherine's persuasive power in the Sala Regia.
insights.speaker: Eloise Davies
insights.so_what: Contrasting reception shows how institutions memorialise their own triumphs.
